strengths: Physics-informed design with zeroth-step Hamiltonian as input descriptor cleverly reduces regression complexity and is well-grounded in DFT theory
Novel E(3)-symmetric architecture maintaining strict symmetry while achieving non-linear expressiveness through TracedGrad mechanism
Large high-quality benchmark dataset (Materials-HAM-SOC) with 17,000 structures spanning 68 elements and explicit spin-orbit coupling effects
Comprehensive methodological framework combining multiple innovations: joint real/reciprocal-space optimization, multi-distance ensemble methods, careful gauge handling
Thorough experimental evaluation including element-wise performance analysis, compelling band structure visualizations, and extensive ablation studies justifying each component
Substantial computational efficiency gains (30-50x speedup vs DFT) enabling practical applications in materials discovery
Clear presentation with extensive appendices providing mathematical rigor, implementation details, and hyperparameter specifications
weaknesses: No comparison with other deep learning methods for Hamiltonian prediction despite citing recent relevant works (Wang et al., Yin et al., Luo et al., etc.) - critical oversight for a methods paper
Evaluation exclusively on single Materials-HAM-SOC dataset with no independent validation set, out-of-distribution testing, or assessment on systems not represented in training data
Dataset composition shows severe imbalance: 59.5% of structures from transition metals (groups 11-30), raising concerns about representation of other chemical families
Ghost state issue incompletely resolved - ablation studies show k-space loss reduces but does not eliminate spurious predictions, with artifacts visible in many cases (Fig. 9)
Hyperparameter selection (λR=0.99955, λQ=0.0001, λPQ=0.00015) poorly justified with minimal explanation of sensitivity and criticality of precise values
Limited scope of validation: only ground-state structures tested, no assessment of generalization to off-center geometries, defects, surfaces, or interfaces
Insufficient justification for design choices: why Gauge MAE over standard MAE, physical intuition for regression target ΔH, connection between trace quantity and ghost states not clearly explained
No demonstration of practical utility for materials discovery - predictions of derived properties (band gaps, carrier mobility, optical properties) not shown
Scalability analysis missing: O(N²) Hamiltonian complexity and memory requirements for large systems (100+ atoms) not discussed
Some counterintuitive ablation results not adequately explained (e.g., Ablation@Loss-PQ performing worse than expected, suggesting potential loss formulation issues)
Band structure visualizations (Fig. 8-9) have overlapping lines making visual evaluation difficult; some subfigures too small to assess effectively

strengths: Novel E(3)-symmetric Transformer architecture with TraceGrad mechanism for joint real-space and k-space Hamiltonian optimization, addressing fundamental challenges in neural network-based electronic structure prediction
Strong empirical results achieving DFT-level accuracy (1.417 meV Gauge MAE) with demonstrated out-of-distribution generalization and >97% computational speedup over traditional DFT
Physically-motivated use of zeroth-step Hamiltonians as input descriptors that are efficiently constructible and provide rich system information
High-quality Materials-HAM-SOC benchmark dataset with 17,000 diverse structures including spin-orbit coupling effects across 60+ elements—valuable resource for the community
Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablation studies, element-wise analysis, and clear demonstration of advantage over DeepH-E3 baseline
Thorough technical treatment with detailed appendices covering DFT background, group theory, implementation details, and loss function derivations enabling reproducibility
Clear physical insights into failure modes (ghost states, error amplification) with principled technical solutions rather than ad-hoc fixes
weaknesses: Overstated 'universality' claims—method limited to periodic crystalline materials, cannot predict from composition alone (requires DFT-calculated H^(0)), and all training data from single source (Materials Project)
Incomplete baseline comparisons—DeepH-E3 comparison limited to monolayer systems (Table 5,7), and no quantitative comparison with other E(3)-equivariant or recent competing methods on same benchmark
Limited generalization analysis—single out-of-distribution element test (Ne) insufficient; no systematic study of performance degradation with compositional complexity or material type variation

Method complexity with many components (4 sub-models, multiple loss terms with tunable weights λR/λQ/λP/λPQ) and incomplete ablations—sensitivity to hyperparameter choices and parametric Clebsch-Gordan benefit not quantified
Dataset limitations—restricted to first 6 periodic table rows, all stable materials from Materials Project, and no explicit scaling analysis for large systems despite O(N) complexity claims
Ghost states and failure modes incompletely analyzed—while mitigation strategy is described, underlying causes and material types where method fails not systematically characterized
Presentation density with critical details (architectural choices, implementation details) relegated to appendices, making main text difficult to follow without constant reference to appendices
